paragraphs.text: Honestly I think my city should put a price on carbon.

Carbon pricing is widely regarded as the most cost-effective instrument for reducing greenhouse gas emissions, because it internalizes the social cost of carbon and allows abatement to occur wherever it is cheapest. By assigning a monetary value to each ton of carbon dioxide emitted, the policy creates a continuous incentive for firms and households to shift toward lower-emission technologies and behaviors. Empirical evaluations of jurisdictions that have implemented such mechanisms indicate measurable reductions in emissions without significant adverse effects on aggregate employment or economic growth.
People always worry it'll just make everything cost more for normal families.

This concern is addressed in the literature through the design of revenue-neutral schemes, in which the proceeds from the levy are returned to residents in the form of per-capita dividends or reductions in other taxes. Under a well-structured dividend program, lower- and middle-income households frequently receive rebates that exceed the additional energy costs they incur, rendering the policy progressive in its net distributional impact. Furthermore, a locally administered price signal can be calibrated to regional conditions and gradually escalated, providing businesses with the predictability necessary to plan long-term capital investments.
So yeah, I think the trade-off is worth it and we should do it.
